questions.q: The sales director's original email request is described in this lesson as being written how?
options: Informal, a little vague, and missing details you'll have to ask about or judge yourself
As a fully specified technical requirements document
As a set of complete user stories with acceptance criteria already written
As a formal Waterfall charter
questions.explain: The lesson deliberately writes the request the way real requests actually arrive — informal and incomplete — because turning that into real backlog items is the actual skill being practiced.

questions.q: What makes a reasonable acceptance criterion for the dashboard's automatic-refresh story?
options: The dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps
The dashboard looks nice
The dashboard was built using Power BI
The dashboard was requested by email
questions.explain: A good acceptance criterion is specific and checkable — stating exactly when fresh data must be available and that no manual steps are involved, not a vague or unrelated statement.

questions.q: What's wrong with a release note that just says 'various improvements'?
options: It isn't specific — a real release note states exactly what changed, why, and anything the audience needs to know
Release notes should never mention what changed
It's too long for most release tracking systems
Nothing is wrong with it — vague release notes are the professional standard
questions.explain: A real release note is short but specific, so both users and the next engineer debugging an issue know exactly what changed and why. 'Various improvements' tells them nothing.

questions.q: When a regional manager reports the dashboard shows zero sales for their region two days after launch, what does this lesson say to do first?
options: Investigate which environment to check and what to look at in the data pipeline, and communicate with the manager while still investigating
Immediately roll back the entire dashboard without investigating
Wait until the issue is fully fixed before telling the regional manager anything
Assume the regional manager made a mistake and take no action
questions.explain: The lesson asks you to think through investigation (which environment, what in the pipeline) and to communicate with the affected user while still investigating, not only after a fix is already in place.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue the capstone is worth doing even on paper, without real SQL or Power BI access?
options: Because it builds the ability to explain how a query's result becomes a backlog item, gets tested, gets signed off, and gets released — not just the ability to write the query itself
Because the technical skills taught in other courses don't matter for a real job
Because interviewers never ask about anything besides syntax
Because production incidents never actually happen in real jobs
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that knowing the technology (SQL, Power BI) is different from being ready for the workflow around it — the whole chain from request to backlog item to test to sign-off to release to incident response.
